summary: Defines new AII TLV structures for pseudowire signaling that allow aggregation of endpoint identifiers, improving scalability and VPN auto-discovery in large networks. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Instead of listing every house on a street, you can list the street, which makes the list short.

questions: what is an attachment individual identifier
how does aii aggregation work in pseudowires
what is the aii type 2 format
subtitle: A new pseudowire endpoint identifier that lets providers summarize thousands of endpoints into one value.

tldr.problem: Pseudowire endpoints have to be identified on both ends, and listing every individual identifier on every provider edge node does not scale in large networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines AII Type 2, a 12-octet value made of a provider-wide Global ID, a 32-bit prefix and a 4-octet attachment circuit ID, so many identifiers can be summarized under one prefix.
tldr.outcome: AII Type 2 gives globally unique identifiers that can be aggregated. It is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 5003 is a Proposed Standard from September 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the pseudowire signaling in RFC 4447.

sections.title: The Endpoint Identifier Problem
sections.content:
RFC 4447 defines how to set up point-to-point pseudowires (PWs) between two provider edge (PE) nodes using LDP signaling. The signaling messages carry a forwarding equivalence class (FEC) element with the PW type and an endpoint identifier, which is used to select the PW forwarder that binds the PW to the attachment circuit at each end.

Two FEC element types exist for this: the PWid FEC (type 128) and the Generalized ID (GID) FEC (type 129). The PWid FEC carries a fixed-length 32-bit value, and the same value must be configured on the local and remote PE before setup. The GID FEC instead carries TLV fields for attachment individual identifiers (AIIs) which, together with an attachment group identifier (AGI), name the endpoints.

The identifier on the local PE is the source attachment identifier (SAI) and the one on the remote PE is the target attachment identifier (TAI). They can differ, which helps when the local PE has to learn remote TAI values first, for example through MP-BGP auto-discovery.
sections.eli5: To connect two ends of a private wire, each end needs a name tag. The old way needed both ends to agree on one number in advance. The newer way lets each end have its own tag.

sections.title: Why Aggregation and Global Uniqueness
sections.content:
The GID FEC lets the AII be structured to suit an application. An AII structure that lets many individual values be identified as one could significantly cut the load on AII distribution mechanisms such as MP-BGP and the memory PEs need to store them. The RFC notes that PWE3 signaling messages will always include a fully qualified AII value.

A globally unique AII would help PW management and security in large inter-AS and inter-provider environments. Providers would not have to worry about AII values overlapping during provisioning, or about AII network address translation boxes during signaling. Such values could aid troubleshooting and could be subjected to source-validity checks. An AII derived automatically from a provider's existing IP address space can simplify provisioning.

The two goals are summarization of many discrete AIIs into a single summary value, and global uniqueness if the provider wants it.
sections.eli5: If many networks pick names on their own, two might pick the same name and cause a mix-up. Giving every name a piece that is unique to its owner prevents that, and grouping names saves space.

sections.title: AII Type 1 and AII Type 2
sections.content:
AII Type 1 had already been allocated by IANA for provisioning models that need a fixed-length 32-bit value. That value is unique on the local PE.

AII Type 2 is the new structure. It allows varying levels of summarization, so it is no longer necessary to distribute or configure every individual AII (which could number in the tens of thousands or more) on local PEs before setting up PWs to remote PEs. How and where the aggregation is done, and how the result is distributed as reachability information, is not covered by this document.

Type 2 combines three things to make globally unique values: a provider's globally unique identifier (Global ID), a 32-bit prefix and a 4-octet attachment circuit identifier (AC ID).
sections.eli5: Type 1 is a plain number that only makes sense inside one building. Type 2 adds the company, the building and the room, so the address works anywhere.

sections.title: The AII Type 2 Layout
sections.content:
The TLV starts with the type, 0x02, and a length, which is the length of the value field in octets and is set to 12. The value has three fields.

  • Global ID: a 4-octet value unique to the provider. It can hold the provider's 2-octet or 4-octet Autonomous System Number (ASN) and is expected to come from the ASN of the autonomous system hosting the PEs. A 2-octet AS number means the two high-order octets MUST be zero. The RFC notes that this use of the ASN has nothing to do with the ASN's role in protocols such as BGP.
  • Prefix: a 32-bit value assigned by the provider, or derived automatically from the PE's /32 IPv4 loopback address. For IP reachability it need not be related to the IPv4 space used in the provider's IGP or BGP.
  • AC ID: a fixed-length 4-octet field that further identifies an attachment circuit on the PE, so circuits that share a prefix can be told apart.
sections.eli5: The tag has three parts: which company, which group of connections, and which single connection inside that group. A big group can be pointed at using only the first two parts.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
AII values appear in AII distribution protocols and in PW signaling protocols, and are subject to various authentication schemes (the RFC names MD5) if desired. Using global ID values such as an ASN in the inter-provider case could allow a form of source-validation checking, to ensure that an AII (aggregated or explicit) came from a legitimate source.

On the IANA side, a value was allocated from the Attachment Individual Identifier (AII) Type registry defined in RFC 4446. The value for this AII type is 0x02.
sections.eli5: Because each tag contains the owner's unique number, a receiver can check that a tag really came from the network it claims to come from.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the value field in octets.

fields.name: Global ID
fields.desc: Unique to the provider; can be derived from the provider's ASN.

fields.name: Prefix
fields.desc: Assigned by the provider or derived from the PE's /32 IPv4 loopback address.

fields.name: AC ID
fields.desc: Identifies an individual attachment circuit that shares a prefix.
